name: Design a Log Aggregation and Search Platform
intent: Collect log lines from thousands of hosts, absorb bursts without losing the errors, and let engineers search by time range and field within seconds at a price the company can afford.
codeTitle: a bounded log buffer with drop policies
finalIntro: One error line travelling from a service to a search result.
prompt: Design a centralized log platform for a company with 2,000 hosts and many teams. Services write log lines to files. Engineers need to search them by time range and by field, such as service or level, within seconds of the line being written. Keep logs for a year, let different teams (tenants) share the platform without hurting each other, and keep the bill under control.
functional: Collect log lines from every host without changing the services
Parse each line into fields and add context such as host, region and service
Search by time range, by field and by words in the message
Keep recent logs fast to search and older logs cheap to keep
Set limits and retention for each tenant
Tail a live stream of matching lines
nonFunctional: A line is searchable within about 10 seconds of being written
Absorb bursts of 5 times the normal volume without losing errors
Handle about 100,000 lines per second on average, 30 MB per second
A slow or broken log platform must never slow or break the services that write logs
Never lose a line silently: if lines are dropped, count them and say so
Keep logs for 30 days in fast storage and for a year in total, at a small fraction of the cost of indexing everything

firstAttempt.text: Each service inserts every log line into one shared SQL table with columns for time, service, level and message. Engineers search with a query using LIKE on the message and a filter on the time.
limits: Each log line costs a database write, so thousands of services writing at once saturate the database and, if the call is synchronous, slow the services too
A burst of logs during an incident is exactly when the database falls over, and the logs of the incident are lost
A LIKE search on the message scans the table, so a search over a week takes minutes
Everything is kept on expensive database storage, with an index, for as long as it is kept at all
One noisy team can fill the table and slow every other team's searches

steps.title: Ship from files with an agent, in batches
steps.problem: Services should not know about the log platform, and a database call for every line is both slow and fragile.
steps.fix: Services keep writing lines to a local file or to standard output, which costs almost nothing. On every host a small agent tails the files, remembers its position (an offset) on disk, collects lines into batches of about a thousand lines or a few seconds, whichever comes first, compresses each batch and sends it to an ingest gateway. If the gateway is down, the agent keeps reading and spools to disk, up to a limit, and sends later. Each batch has an id, so a repeated batch can be recognised.
steps.tradeoff: Services are decoupled from the platform, and one request carries a thousand lines, which is far cheaper than a thousand requests. A batch waits a few seconds to fill, so lines are never instant, and the agent adds some CPU and memory on every host.

steps.title: Put a durable queue between collecting and storing
steps.problem: Logs come in bursts. An incident multiplies the volume by five at the moment the search store is under most pressure, and if the store cannot keep up, lines are lost.
steps.fix: The ingest gateway does little more than authenticate the batch and append it to a replicated queue, partitioned by tenant and source, and acknowledge it. Consumers read from the queue at their own pace, so a burst becomes a backlog instead of a failure. The queue is sized to hold some time, such as half an hour, of peak traffic. The agent moves its offset only after the acknowledgement, so delivery is at-least-once.
steps.tradeoff: Bursts are absorbed and downstream outages do not lose data. The cost is extra delay when there is a backlog, a cluster to run, and duplicates, which the next stages must tolerate. A queue is not infinite: when it is full, something has to give.

steps.title: Parse, enrich and clean each line
steps.problem: Raw lines are text of every shape. Searching by field is only possible once the fields have been extracted, and some lines contain data that must not be stored.
steps.fix: A pool of parsers reads from the queue. Lines that are already structured (JSON) are read directly, and others are parsed with a pattern chosen by service. Each line is given a standard timestamp, level and service, and enriched with the host, region, version and tenant. Known secrets and card numbers are redacted, and lines that cannot be parsed are kept as raw text with a flag, rather than dropped. Duplicates are removed using the batch id and the offset.
steps.tradeoff: Fields are consistent and sensitive data stays out of storage, and parsers scale independently. Parsing costs CPU, a bad pattern can mislabel millions of lines, and structured logging at the source is cheaper and more reliable than guessing the structure later.

steps.title: Index only what you search by, and keep the text in cheap storage
steps.problem: Indexing every word of every line in an inverted index is fast to search but makes the index as large as the data, and at 2.6 TB of logs a day the cost is out of reach.
steps.fix: Split the work. A small index holds only labels (service, level, tenant, region) and the time range of each chunk, and the lines themselves are compressed into chunks in object storage, written in time order per label set. A query uses the time range and the labels to find the few chunks that can match, and then scans those chunks for the words in the message. A full inverted index over the message stays available, for a short window or for selected services that need instant free-text search.
steps.tradeoff: Storage and indexing cost fall several times over (about 7 times in the estimate here), since compressed text is a fraction of an index. A search by an unlabelled word must scan chunks, so it is slower than an inverted index lookup but is spread over many workers. Labels must have a small number of values, or the small index stops being small.

steps.title: Move data through hot, warm and cold tiers
steps.problem: Almost every search is about the last hour or day, and almost no one searches last year's debug lines, yet all of them cost the same to keep.
steps.fix: Data ages through tiers. Hot is the last few days, on fast disks with a cache, for instant searches. Warm is the rest of the month, in object storage with only the small index. Cold is the remainder of the year, in a cheap archive tier, and a search of cold data is a job that may take minutes. Retention is set per tenant, and deleting old data means deleting whole chunks by date, which is cheap. Queries must always carry a time range, so the system knows which tiers to look at.
steps.tradeoff: The bill is dominated by the small hot tier instead of the whole year. Old data is slower to get, tier moves have to be automated, and regulations may require deleting a user's data from every tier, which time-ordered chunks make awkward.

steps.title: Limit each tenant, sample, and decide what to drop
steps.problem: One service with a debug flag left on can send ten times the normal volume, fill the queue and push out everyone else's logs. When the platform is overloaded something will be dropped, and by default it is the wrong thing.
steps.fix: The gateway meters every tenant with a rate limit and a quota, sets a bucket of burst allowance, and counts what it refuses. When the queue passes a threshold the platform applies a drop policy by level: debug is sampled first, then info, and warnings and errors are kept as long as there is any room, evicting lower levels to make space. Every drop is counted per tenant and level and shown as a metric, so a loss is visible, and the agent gets a response telling it to slow down. Alerts fire on the drop counters and on the ingestion delay.
steps.tradeoff: One tenant cannot take the platform down, and in an overload the lines that matter survive. Teams will see sampled debug logs and must be told, and the sampling rules need an owner. A bigger buffer only moves the problem from lost lines to late lines.

failures.scenario: A bad deploy makes one service log 100 times more
failures.impact: The queue fills in minutes, other tenants' lines are delayed or dropped, and the bill spikes.
failures.answer: The tenant's rate limit refuses the excess at the gateway, and the refused lines are counted. Sampling thins its debug and info lines, errors are kept, and an alert tells the team that their quota is exhausted. Other tenants see no change because each tenant has its own share of the queue.

failures.scenario: The indexing cluster is down for an hour
failures.impact: Nothing new becomes searchable, and the queue grows.
failures.answer: The queue holds the backlog, since it is sized for at least half an hour of peak traffic, and the agents spool to disk if it fills. When the cluster returns, the consumers catch up, and a lag alert has been firing the whole time. If the outage is longer than the buffer, the drop policy keeps errors and counts the lost debug lines.

failures.scenario: An agent restarts or a log file is rotated while it is reading
failures.impact: Lines could be read twice or skipped.
failures.answer: The agent stores the offset together with the identity of the file (its inode), so after a restart it resumes where it stopped and recognises a rotated file as a new one, finishing the old one first. A line sent twice is removed by the batch id and offset downstream, so delivery is at-least-once with duplicates removed.

failures.scenario: A service logs a credit card number or a password
failures.impact: Sensitive data is copied into a system that many people can search, and it will be kept for a year.
failures.answer: Redaction rules in the parser mask known patterns before the line is stored, and access to logs is limited by tenant and role. The leak is also a bug in the service, so a scan finds the offending code and the old chunks are deleted. Encrypting stored chunks limits the damage of a storage leak but not of an overly broad search permission.

alternatives.title: How to index

options.name: Full inverted index of every word
options.pro: Instant free-text search on any word
options.con: The index is as big as the data and the ingest is CPU-heavy, so cost grows in step with volume

options.name: Labels only index over compressed chunks
options.pro: Very cheap to write and to keep, with fast filters by service, level and time
options.con: Free-text search scans the matching chunks, and high-cardinality labels break it

options.name: No index, grep at query time
options.pro: Nothing to maintain at write time
options.con: Every search reads everything in the time range, which only works at small scale

alternatives.pick: A labels-and-time index over object-storage chunks, with a full inverted index only for a short window or selected services.

alternatives.title: What to do when the buffer is full

options.name: Drop the newest lines
options.pro: Simple and cheap, since the queue is untouched
options.con: Loses the latest lines, which in an incident are the most useful, with no regard to level

options.name: Drop the oldest lines
options.pro: Keeps what is freshest, and the buffer never blocks
options.con: Erases the start of the incident, which usually holds the cause

options.name: Sample by level and keep errors
options.pro: Debug is thinned first and errors survive as long as possible
options.con: More rules to explain, and debug lines may be thinned even when the burst would have fitted

options.name: Block the writers
options.con: A logging problem now stops the services, which is not acceptable

alternatives.pick: Sample by level, count every drop, and never block the writer.

alternatives.title: Where to parse

options.name: In the agent on the host
options.pro: Distributes the work and shrinks what travels
options.con: Hard to change patterns on thousands of hosts, and it uses CPU of the services' machines

options.name: In central parsers after the queue
options.pro: One place to fix and test, scales with the backlog
options.con: Central CPU cost, and raw lines travel over the network

alternatives.pick: Central parsers, with light work (multiline joining, labels) in the agent.

alternatives.title: How lines reach the platform

options.name: Agent tails files
options.pro: Services stay unchanged, and logs survive a platform outage on disk
options.con: An agent to deploy and update on every host

options.name: Services send over the network
options.pro: No file handling, and low delay
options.con: Logs are lost when the platform is down, and services are coupled to it

alternatives.pick: Agents tailing files or container output.

quiz.question: Services insert every log line straight into a shared SQL table. During an incident the volume is five times higher, the database falls over, and the incident's own logs are lost while services slow down. What is the best change?
options: Move the table to a much larger database machine with more memory and faster disks, sized for five times the normal write rate of the platform
Let services write to local files, with a host agent that ships batches of about a thousand lines to a gateway that appends to a replicated queue
Make each insert asynchronous inside the service, with an in-memory buffer that is flushed to the database in the background by a worker thread
Shard the log table by service name across several database machines, so that each machine takes a fraction of the write load at the peak
quiz.explanation: Files cost almost nothing to write, the agent batches lines and keeps its offset, and the queue turns a burst into a backlog rather than a failure. A bigger database still fails at the next burst. An in-memory buffer inside the service is lost on a crash and still couples the service to the platform.

quiz.question: Normal traffic is 30 MB per second. Bursts reach 5 times that and can last 30 minutes. Consumers keep draining at 30 MB per second during a burst. How much queue storage is needed to absorb a burst without dropping lines?
options: About 216 GB, which is the excess of 120 MB per second over 1,800 seconds
About 270 GB, which is 150 MB per second over 1,800 seconds
About 54 GB, which is 30 MB per second over 1,800 seconds
About 540 GB, which is 150 MB per second over a full hour
quiz.explanation: The queue grows only by what arrives above what consumers drain: (150 - 30) MB per second times 1,800 seconds is 216 GB. 270 GB ignores the draining. 54 GB is just half an hour of normal volume. In practice the queue is also replicated, so raw disk is a multiple of this.

quiz.question: A tenant leaves a debug flag on and sends ten times its usual volume. The queue is at 90% and another tenant is in the middle of an incident with many error lines. Which response protects the platform and the logs that matter most?
options: Drop the oldest lines in the queue to make room for new ones, since the freshest lines are the most useful ones for the engineers during an incident
Block the writers by making the agents refuse new lines until the queue has drained, so that nothing is ever lost for any tenant on the platform
Rate-limit the noisy tenant at the gateway and count what is refused. If the queue still fills, sample debug and info first and keep errors.
Double the queue size and the number of consumers, so that the extra volume is simply absorbed and no tenant has to be limited at all by anyone
quiz.explanation: A per-tenant quota stops one tenant from pushing out others, and a level-based drop policy keeps errors as long as there is room, with every drop counted. Dropping the oldest lines erases the start of the incident. Blocking writers would let a logging problem slow the services, and a bigger buffer only changes lost lines into late ones.
